question: The EU has worked closely alongside all UN members to achieve a global digital pact outlining principles, objectives and actions to promote the digital transition of societies.

1 However, it has been observed that the over-reliance on digital services promoted by the EU and several Member States may expose European societies to serious risks when internet access is unavailable for long periods, as recently happened in Spain and Portugal.

Among the infrastructures that were put out of service were, on the one hand, online banking and, on the other, credit institution ATMs, making it impossible for citizens who did not have cash to purchase essential daily items.2 In light of the above, the Commission is asked: 1.
Is the complete abolition of cash from the European legal order, as promoted by some Member States, in line with European law?3

Does the Commission have a strategy - or even a framework of recommendations - to address crises in which European citizens are unable to access their bank accounts to purchase essential goods using online banking or ATMs?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2025) Euro cash has legal tender status in the euro area under EU Law. Its continued existence and availability is guaranteed by the Treaties, as long as there is demand for it. On 28 June 2023, the Commission put forward a legislative proposal on the legal tender of cash aiming at ensuring the widespread acceptance of and access to cash.

This proposal seeks to ensure that euro cash remains widely accepted for payments and easily accessible for people, businesses and public entities across the euro area. It obliges Member States to monitor and report on the situation and take measures to address any problems identified in relation to cash acceptance and access.

The proposal will ensure that everyone in the euro area is free to choose their preferred payment method and has access to basic cash services, thereby also ensuring the financial inclusion of vulnerable groups who tend to rely more on cash payments.

The Communication on the European Preparedness Union Strategy1 adopted by the Commission on 26 March 2025 sets out a comprehensive approach to preparedness calling for involvement of public authorities, society and individuals in building a culture of resilience to crises, whether they be natural or man-made disasters or conflicts.

In these circumstances the role of cash and the cash infrastructure is key, thus it is essential to ensure that Member States are prepared appropriately to respond in different exceptional circumstances where the demand for cash could rapidly increase or cashless payments are significantly disrupted.
